item.title: AI Architect Learning Path
item.description: About four weeks at one to two hours a day covers the whole path. If you have less time, read the two case studies and the Review section first, then fill gaps from the linked articles.

item.title: AI Engineering Fundamentals: From Models to Products
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI engineering is the discipline of building applications on top of foundation models that someone else has usually trained. Instead of collecting data and training a model first, you start from a model that already works, then adapt it — with prompts, context, tools, fine-tuning — and wrap it in the product, evaluation and operations it needs.

item.title: AI Architecture Review Framework
item.description:
Why a review framework#

AI designs fail in predictable places: unclear success criteria, missing permissions in retrieval, agents with too much autonomy, no evaluation, no cost model. A shared framework lets architects, security, risk and product owners review any AI design — your own before you build it, or a team’s at an architecture board — consistently and quickly.

item.title: The AI Agent Framework Landscape
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent framework is a library or SDK that implements the plumbing every agent needs — the loop that calls the model, executes tools and feeds results back — plus state, memory, multi-agent coordination, human-in-the-loop, guardrails and tracing. You write the instructions, tools and business logic; the framework runs them.

item.title: RAG Fundamentals: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) answers a question in two steps: first retrieve the most relevant pieces of your own documents, then ask the LLM to generate an answer using those pieces as context.

Analogy: an open-book exam. The model is a smart student who has not read your company handbook. RAG hands them the right pages before they answer.

item.title: Spring AI Fundamentals
item.description:
Simple definition#

Spring AI is the Spring project for building AI applications in Java. It gives you portable APIs for chat, embeddings, images, audio and vector stores across many providers, plus higher-level building blocks — a fluent ChatClient, advisors for RAG and memory, tool calling, MCP, structured output and observability — all configured the Spring Boot way.

item.title: What Is an AI Agent?
item.description:
Simple definition#

An AI agent is a system where an LLM decides what to do next, does it by calling tools, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is reached or it must stop.

A chatbot answers. An agent acts: it can look up an order, check a policy, issue a refund, and email the customer — choosing the steps itself.

item.title: Chunking and Embeddings
item.description:
Simple definition#

  • Chunking is splitting documents into smaller passages so that search can return just the relevant part, and so it fits in the prompt.
  • An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning have vectors that are close together.

Together they decide what your RAG system can find.

item.title: How Large Language Models Work
item.description:
Simple definition#

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to predict the next piece of text. Given “The capital of France is”, it assigns a probability to every possible next token and “Paris” scores highest. Repeating that prediction one token at a time produces sentences, code, plans and answers.

item.title: From Generative to Agentic AI: Five Levels, SPAR and the Three Keystones
item.description:
Simple definition#

Generative AI produces content when asked. Agentic AI pursues a goal: it plans, uses tools, takes actions across systems, remembers, and improves from results — with as little human prompting as the task allows.

item.title: Python and TypeScript Agent Frameworks
item.description:
How to read this page#

Each profile answers the same questions: what is the core idea, what does minimal code look like, what is it good at, and what should you watch out for. Code is deliberately minimal and uses a placeholder MODEL; check each project’s documentation for current model identifiers and options.

item.title: Review Questions: Enterprise and Agentic AI
item.description:
Answers are deliberately short — enough to check your understanding. Each section links to the article with the full explanation.

TipHow to use this page

Cover the answer, explain it in your own words, then compare. Mark questions you hesitated on and reread the linked article.

item.title: RAG with Spring AI
item.description:
What we are building#

A Spring Boot service that ingests policy documents into PostgreSQL with pgvector, then answers questions with citations, filtered by the user’s department.

Dependencies and configuration#

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-starter-vector-store-pgvector</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-vector-store-advisor</artifactId>    <!-- QuestionAnswerAdvisor -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-rag</artifactId>                     <!-- RetrievalAugmentationAdvisor -->
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.ai</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-ai-pdf-document-reader</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- plus a chat model starter and an embedding model starter, e.g. OpenAI or Bedrock -->

spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/assistant
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.initialize-schema=true
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.index-type=HNSW
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.distance-type=COSINE_DISTANCE
spring.ai.vectorstore.pgvector.dimensions=1536

The starter auto-configures a VectorStore bean using the EmbeddingModel bean from your embedding starter. In production, prefer creating the schema with your migration tool (Flyway/Liquibase) and set initialize-schema=false.

item.title: Agent Frameworks for Java, Kotlin and .NET
item.description:
Why JVM-native agents matter#

Most enterprise systems of record — banking cores, insurance platforms, ERP integrations — run on the JVM or .NET. Building agents in the same stack reuses existing security (Spring Security, OAuth), transactions, data access, messaging, observability and deployment pipelines, and keeps agents close to the services they call. Since 2025 the JVM has gained a real choice of agent frameworks.

item.title: Enterprise AI Quick Reference
item.description:
Numbers to know#

Item Rule of thumb
Token ↔ text 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 English words; 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words ≈ 1.5 pages
Output vs input price Output tokens typically cost 3–5× input tokens
Prompt caching Cached input often ~90% cheaper; needs a stable prefix
Batch APIs ~50% cheaper; results within hours
Generation speed Tens to a few hundred tokens/s depending on model and load
Total latency ≈ TTFT + output tokens ÷ tokens per second
Context windows ~128K to 1M+ tokens on current frontier models
Weights memory Parameters × bytes per parameter (FP16 = 2, INT8 = 1, INT4 = 0.5); 70B FP16 ≈ 140 GB
Vector storage vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes (float32); +~50% for HNSW graph
Chunk size 300–800 tokens, 10–20% overlap, plus heading context
Retrieval Retrieve 20–100 candidates → rerank → send 3–8
Golden dataset Start with 50–100 cases, grow to several hundred
Error compounding 0.95 per step over 10 steps ≈ 60% success

Cost formula#

monthly cost = requests/month × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price)
peak TPM     = peak requests/min × (input + output tokens per request)

Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning#

Need Use
Task definition, format, tone Prompting (+ few-shot)
Private, fresh, citable, permissioned knowledge RAG
Consistent behaviour, domain style, cheaper small model Fine-tuning (LoRA)
Actions and live data Tools / agents

RAG pipeline at a glance#

Top upgrades by impact: parsing & structure-aware chunking → hybrid search → reranking → metadata/ACL filters → query rewriting → contextual retrieval → agentic/graph retrieval.

item.title: Agents with Spring AI: Tools, MCP and Memory
item.description:
What this article covers#

How the agent concepts from Module 3 map to Spring AI 2.0 code:

Concept Spring AI
Tool @Tool method, ToolCallback
Identity passed to tools ToolContext
Agent loop Built-in tool execution in ChatClient, or ToolCallingAdvisor
MCP client spring-ai-starter-mcp-client → tools as ToolCallbackProvider
MCP server spring-ai-starter-mcp-server-webmvc + @McpTool
Short-term memory ChatMemory + MessageChatMemoryAdvisor
Persistent memory JdbcChatMemoryRepository (and Redis, Cassandra, Mongo, Neo4j)

Tools with @Tool#

@Component
class OrderTools {

    private final OrderService orders;

    OrderTools(OrderService orders) { this.orders = orders; }

    @Tool(description = """
        Get status, items and delivery estimate of one of the current customer's orders.
        Use when the customer asks where an order is. Order numbers look like A-12345.""")
    OrderView getOrder(@ToolParam(description = "Order number, e.g. A-12345") String orderId,
                       ToolContext ctx) {
        String customerId = (String) ctx.getContext().get("customerId"); // from session, not the model
        return orders.findForCustomer(orderId, customerId)
                     .orElseThrow(() -> new ToolException("Order not found for this customer"));
    }

    @Tool(description = "Refund an order of the current customer. Amount in EUR.")
    RefundResult refund(String orderId, BigDecimal amount, String reason, ToolContext ctx) {
        String customerId = (String) ctx.getContext().get("customerId");
        return orders.requestRefund(orderId, customerId, amount, reason); // limits enforced here
    }
}

String reply = chatClient.prompt()
    .user(customerMessage)
    .tools(orderTools)
    .toolContext(Map.of("customerId", authenticatedCustomerId))
    .call()
    .content();
  • Spring AI generates JSON Schemas from method signatures; @ToolParam adds descriptions and required flags.
  • ToolContext passes data to the tool without sending it to the model — use it for identity, tenant and correlation IDs.
  • returnDirect = true on @Tool returns the result to the caller without another model round trip.
  • Exceptions can be converted into messages for the model so it can recover; keep them short and helpful. (ToolException above stands for your own exception type.)
  • Enforce business limits in OrderService, not in the prompt.

The tool-calling loop#

By default the tool loop runs inside the model call. In Spring AI 2.0 you can instead add ToolCallingAdvisor, which runs the loop inside the advisor chain, so other advisors (logging, memory, guardrails, auditing) see every iteration — useful for agent observability and per-step policy checks.

item.title: Tool Calling (Function Calling)
item.description:
Simple definition#

Tool calling (also called function calling) lets an LLM ask your application to run a function. You describe the available tools; the model replies with “call get_order with {"orderId": "8812"}”; your code runs it and sends the result back; the model continues.

item.title: Foundation Models: Training Data, Scaling, Post-Training and Sampling
item.description:
Simple definition#

A foundation model is the product of three choices: what data it learned from, how big it is and how long it was trained, and how it was post-trained to behave like an assistant. A fourth choice — how you sample from it — is yours, at inference time.

item.title: Vector Databases Explained
item.description:
Simple definition#

A vector database stores embeddings (vectors) together with their text and metadata, and answers one question fast: “which stored vectors are closest to this query vector?” — usually with filters such as “only documents this user may see”.

item.title: Advanced RAG: Hybrid Search, Reranking, Query Transformation and Agentic RAG
item.description:
Simple definition#

Advanced RAG adds steps before, during and after retrieval to find better context: fix the question (pre-retrieval), search in more than one way (retrieval), and filter and order what was found (post-retrieval). Agentic RAG goes further and lets an LLM decide when, where and how many times to search.

item.title: LLM Inference, Latency and Cost
item.description:
Simple definition#

Inference is running a trained model to produce output. For an LLM it has two phases: reading the whole prompt (prefill) and then generating the answer one token at a time (decode). Almost every latency, throughput and cost decision in an AI system traces back to these two phases.

item.title: Managed Agent Platforms and Low-Code Builders
item.description:
Simple definition#

A managed agent platform runs agents for you. You bring agent code written with almost any framework; the platform provides an isolated, scalable runtime, managed memory, identity for agents, a tool gateway that turns APIs into MCP tools, sandboxed browser and code tools, and observability — the operational layer most teams would otherwise build on Kubernetes.

item.title: Agent Planning, Tool Selection and Failure Modes
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent is defined by two things: the environment it operates in and the tools it can use. Planning is how it turns a goal into a sequence of tool calls; reflection is how it notices mistakes and corrects them.

item.title: Spring AI in Production
item.description:
What changes in production#

A demo calls a model and prints the answer. A production service must be observable (what did it do, how long, at what cost), tested (evaluated on a dataset), resilient (timeouts, retries, fallbacks), secure and governed. Spring AI plugs into the Spring Boot production toolkit you already use for this.

item.title: AI Security: OWASP LLM Top 10, Prompt Injection and Agent Security
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI security protects AI systems — models, prompts, data, tools and agents — from being manipulated, leaking information, or being used to cause harm. Classic application security still applies; LLMs add a new problem: instructions and data travel in the same channel (natural language), so data can act like code.

item.title: GraphRAG and Knowledge Graphs
item.description:
Simple definition#

A knowledge graph stores facts as entities (nodes: people, products, systems, contracts) and relationships (edges: owns, depends on, supplies). GraphRAG uses such a graph — often built automatically from documents by an LLM — to retrieve connected facts and summaries that plain vector search cannot find.

item.title: Inference Optimisation: Making Models Faster and Cheaper
item.description:
Simple definition#

Inference optimisation is making a model produce the same (or nearly the same) output faster, cheaper or for more users at once. It happens at three levels: the model (make it smaller or decode smarter), the hardware (use the accelerator well) and the service (schedule requests well).

item.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
item.description:
Simple definition#

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data. An MCP server exposes capabilities — tools to call, resources to read, prompt templates to use — and any MCP-compatible AI application can discover and use them.

item.title: AI Governance and Responsible AI
item.description:
Simple definition#

AI governance is the set of policies, roles, processes and technical controls that make sure an organisation’s AI is lawful, safe, fair, secure, transparent and accountable — and that someone is answerable for each system. Responsible AI names the principles; governance is how you put them into practice.

item.title: Prompt and Context Engineering
item.description:
Simple definition#

Prompt engineering is writing the instructions and examples that steer an LLM toward the output you need. Context engineering is the broader discipline of deciding everything that goes into the context window on each call — instructions, retrieved documents, memory, tool results — and in what order.

item.title: Evaluating RAG and LLM Applications
item.description:
Simple definition#

Evaluation is measuring how well your AI system does its job, on a fixed set of test cases, with repeatable scores. For RAG you measure two things separately: did we find the right information (retrieval), and did we use it correctly (generation)?

item.title: Agentic Workflow Patterns
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agentic patterns are reusable shapes for combining LLM calls, tools and code — the “design patterns” of AI systems. Most production systems are a composition of a few of them. They range from fully code-controlled workflows to fully model-controlled agents.

item.title: System Design: Enterprise Knowledge Assistant (RAG)
item.description:
The design brief#

“Design an AI assistant that lets 50,000 employees ask questions about internal policies, procedures and technical documentation, with answers grounded in company documents.”

This walk-through follows the AI system design framework.

1. Requirements#

Functional

item.title: Multi-Agent Systems
item.description:
Simple definition#

A multi-agent system splits work among several agents, each with its own instructions, tools and context, which coordinate to reach a goal. It is the AI equivalent of a team: a lead delegates to specialists.

item.title: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning
item.description:
Simple definition#

There are three main ways to make a general-purpose LLM useful for your business:

  • Prompting — change the instructions the model receives.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) — change the knowledge the model receives, by retrieving relevant documents into the prompt.
  • Fine-tuning — change the model’s weights by training it further on your examples.

A useful slogan: RAG for knowledge, fine-tuning for behaviour, prompting for everything first.

item.title: Fine-Tuning in Depth: Memory, PEFT, LoRA and Model Merging
item.description:
Simple definition#

Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own examples so that it changes its behaviour — format, style, task skill, domain vocabulary. It is the most powerful adaptation technique and the most expensive one to run and maintain.

item.title: Agent Memory, State and Durable Execution
item.description:
Simple definition#

LLMs are stateless: each call knows only what is in its prompt. Memory is everything your system stores and feeds back so an agent can continue a conversation, remember a user’s preferences, learn from past cases, and resume a long task after a crash.

item.title: Dataset Engineering: Curating, Synthesising and Processing Data
item.description:
Simple definition#

Dataset engineering is the work of producing the data a model is trained or evaluated on: deciding what data you need, getting it, generating it when you cannot get it, and cleaning it into a usable format.

item.title: Agent Reliability, Guardrails and Evaluation
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agent reliability is the engineering that makes an agent do the right thing consistently, stop when it should, and fail safely when it cannot succeed. It combines guardrails (prevent bad actions), budgets (bound cost and time), evaluation (measure behaviour before and after release) and observability (see what happened).

item.title: The Agent Protocol Stack: MCP, A2A, AG-UI, Agent Skills and AGENTS.md
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agents need to talk to three kinds of counterpart: tools and data, other agents, and people through a user interface. Since 2024 an open standard has emerged for each, plus two lightweight file conventions for giving agents know-how and instructions:

item.title: Evaluation Methodology: How to Measure Foundation Models
item.description:
Simple definition#

Evaluation methodology is the toolbox of ways to score a model’s output. There are four families: language-modelling metrics (how well the model predicts text), exact evaluation (checks with an unambiguous answer), AI as a judge (another model scores the output) and comparative evaluation (rank models by which output people or judges prefer).

item.title: Evaluating AI Systems: Criteria, Benchmarks and the Evaluation Pipeline
item.description:
Simple definition#

Evaluating an AI system means checking whether the whole application — prompts, retrieval, model, tools and guardrails — does its job well enough, safely enough and cheaply enough. It turns the methods in evaluation methodology into a repeatable pipeline that runs before every change and continuously in production.

item.title: Agent Harnesses, Skills and Long-Running Agents
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agent harness is everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, tools, permissions, context management, memory files, sub-agents, skills, checkpoints and verification. Two agents using the same model can perform very differently because of their harnesses — which is why “harness engineering” became a discipline of its own in 2025–2026.

item.title: Computer-Use and Browser Agents
item.description:
Simple definition#

A computer-use agent operates software the way a person does: it looks at the screen (screenshots or the page structure), decides what to click or type, performs the action, and repeats. Browser agents are the web-only variant. They let agents work with applications that have no API.

item.title: Model Selection for the Enterprise
item.description:
Simple definition#

Model selection is choosing which LLM (or which mix of LLMs) serves each use case, based on quality for the task, cost, latency, data-protection requirements and operational fit. In an enterprise it is not a one-time choice: models change every few months, so the architecture must make swapping cheap.

item.title: Agent Identity and Access Control
item.description:
Simple definition#

Agent identity and access control answers three questions for every action an agent takes: who is acting (the agent, the user, or both), what are they allowed to do, and how can we prove later what happened. Agents are a new kind of non-human identity that often act on behalf of a human, so classic service-account thinking is not enough.

item.title: The Enterprise AI Stack: Reference Architecture
item.description:
Simple definition#

The enterprise AI stack is the set of shared layers an organisation builds so that many teams can ship AI features safely and cheaply: access to models, a gateway to control that access, pipelines that turn company data into retrievable knowledge, frameworks for chains and agents, and the operations, security and governance around all of it.

item.title: Agentic AI Strategy and Operating Model
item.description:
Simple definition#

An agentic AI strategy decides where agents should do work in the organisation, how much autonomy they get, what platform they run on, how value and risk are measured, and how people and processes change around them. It turns isolated pilots into a governed, scalable capability.

item.title: AI Engineering Architecture: Building It Up Step by Step
item.description:
Simple definition#

Most AI applications converge on the same architecture, but no team should build it all on day one. This article grows it one component at a time, each added only when a concrete need appears: context, guardrails, routing, caching, actions — and the observability that makes all of it operable.

item.title: A Practical Playbook for Building AI Agents: Opportunity Scoring and the A.G.E.N.T. Framework
item.description:
Simple definition#

This playbook covers the practical path from “we should use agents” to an agent that works in production: find the right opportunity, score and prioritise it, design the agent with a structured framework, and implement it with principles that avoid the most common failures.

item.title: Designing for User Feedback and the Data Flywheel
item.description:
Simple definition#

User feedback is every signal users give — deliberately or not — about whether the application helped them. It is the one data source competitors cannot copy. Collected well, it drives evaluation (are we getting better?), development (what should we train or fix next?) and personalisation (what does this user prefer?).

item.title: On-Premise and Hybrid GenAI Deployment
item.description:
Simple definition#

Deployment topology decides where each part of a GenAI system runs: the model, the retrieval index, the orchestration code and the logs. On-premise means inference runs on hardware you operate; hybrid means some workloads run on your hardware or private cloud and others call cloud-hosted models, with one control plane deciding which request goes where.

item.title: LLMOps: Running AI in Production
item.description:
Simple definition#

LLMOps is the set of practices for building, deploying, monitoring and improving LLM applications in production. It extends DevOps and MLOps with things specific to LLMs: prompts as versioned artefacts, evaluation of non-deterministic output, token cost, safety guardrails and traces of multi-step chains and agents.

item.title: GenAI Adoption Strategy for the Enterprise
item.description:
Simple definition#

A GenAI adoption strategy decides where generative AI should create value, which capabilities the organisation buys or builds, which models and deployments it standardises on, how risk is governed, and how people and processes change — so that AI moves from scattered experiments to a measured, repeatable capability.

item.title: Hybrid AI in Financial Services: Practical Decisions
item.description:
Simple definition#

In financial services, hybrid AI means running each AI workload in the place its data, regulation and economics allow: frontier models through in-region cloud for tasks that need the best reasoning, open-weight or licensed models on the bank’s own infrastructure for restricted data and high-volume work, and one governed control plane across both.

item.title: System Design: Agentic Customer-Support Platform
item.description:
The design brief#

“Design an AI agent for an e-commerce company that resolves customer-support requests — order status, returns, refunds, address changes — over chat and email, escalating to humans when needed.”

1. Requirements#

Functional

item.title: About this handbook
item.description:
Purpose#

The Enterprise AI & Agentic AI Knowledge Hub explains strategic AI architecture simply, for architects and senior engineers who design, build or govern AI systems — and for anyone who wants to review and test their understanding of enterprise AI. It is the companion to the Java & Software Architecture Knowledge Hub.

item.title: Glossary
item.description:
Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanation.

A#

A2A (Agent2Agent protocol)
An open protocol for agents to discover each other through agent cards and delegate tasks. See Multi-agent systems.
AG-UI (Agent–User Interaction protocol)
An open protocol streaming typed events between an agent and a user interface. See Agent protocol stack.
Advisor (Spring AI)
An interceptor around a ChatClient call, used for memory, RAG, logging, tool loops and custom concerns. See Spring AI fundamentals.
Agent
An LLM-driven system that loops — reason, act through tools, observe — until a goal is met. See What is an agent?
Agent framework
A library that runs the agent loop and adds state, tools, multi-agent coordination, guardrails and tracing. See Framework landscape.
Agent harness
Everything around the model that makes an agent reliable: loop, tools, permissions, context management, skills, checkpoints, verification. See Harnesses & skills.
Agent Skills
Folders with a SKILL.md and resources that agents load on demand. See Agent protocol stack.
AGENTS.md
A Markdown file in a repository with instructions for coding agents. See Agent protocol stack.
Agentic RAG
RAG where an agent decides when and where to retrieve, possibly several times. See Advanced retrieval.
AI gateway
The single controlled entry point to all models: auth, quotas, guardrails, routing, caching, logging, cost. See Enterprise AI stack.
ANN (approximate nearest neighbour)
Search that finds most of the closest vectors quickly without comparing all of them. See Vector databases.
Attention
The transformer mechanism by which each token weighs and uses information from other tokens. See How LLMs work.
AgentOps
Operating agents like production services: SLOs, monitoring, incidents, cost and continuous evaluation. See Agentic AI strategy.
Air-gapped deployment
Running models with no network path to the outside; updates imported offline. See On-prem & hybrid.
A.G.E.N.T. framework
A five-part agent design checklist: agent identity, gear and brain, execution and workflow, navigation and rules, testing and trust. See Agent building playbook.
AI engineering
Building applications on top of foundation models — adapting and evaluating an existing model rather than training one. See AI engineering fundamentals.
Agentic AI progression
Six levels from manual work (0) through rule-based and intelligent automation to agentic workflows (3), semi-autonomous (4) and fully autonomous agents (5). See Levels, SPAR & keystones.

B–C#

BM25
A classic keyword relevance ranking function used in sparse/keyword search. See Advanced retrieval.
Chunking
Splitting documents into passages for retrieval. See Chunking and embeddings.
Computer-use agent
An agent that operates graphical interfaces from screenshots with clicks and keystrokes. See Computer-use agents.
Context engineering
Deciding everything that goes into the context window on each call. See Prompt and context engineering.
Context window
The maximum tokens (input + output) a model processes per call. See How LLMs work.
Contextual retrieval
Prepending an LLM-written situating sentence to each chunk before indexing. See Advanced retrieval.
Cross-encoder / reranker
A model that scores a query and a document together for precise relevance. See Advanced retrieval.
Data-classification routing
An AI gateway choosing the allowed model deployment by the highest data class in the assembled prompt. See On-prem & hybrid.
Comparative evaluation
Ranking models from pairwise “which is better?” judgements aggregated with Elo or Bradley–Terry. See Evaluation methodology.
Continuous batching
A serving scheduler that adds and removes requests from the running batch at every decode step. See Inference optimisation.

D–E#

Distillation
Training a small model on a large model’s outputs. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.
Embedding
A vector representing the meaning of text. See Chunking and embeddings.
EU AI Act
The EU regulation classifying AI systems by risk tier with matching obligations. See AI governance.
Evaluator–optimizer
A loop where one LLM generates and another critiques until criteria are met. See Workflow patterns.
Embabel
A JVM agent framework on Spring AI that plans typed actions toward goals with GOAP. See JVM frameworks.
Excessive agency
An LLM system with more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs. See AI security.
Data contamination
Benchmark or evaluation examples leaking into training data, inflating scores. See Evaluating AI systems.
Data flywheel
More users produce more feedback and data, which improve the product and attract more users. See User feedback.
Dataset engineering
Curating, synthesising, deduplicating and formatting the data used to fine-tune and evaluate models. See Dataset engineering.
Degenerate feedback loop
When a system’s outputs shape the feedback that trains it, amplifying its own biases (popularity bias, sycophancy). See User feedback.
DPO (direct preference optimisation)
Preference fine-tuning directly on (preferred, rejected) response pairs, without a separate reward model. See Training, scaling & sampling.
Evaluation-driven development
Defining evaluation criteria and data before building, like tests before code. See Evaluating AI systems.
Functional correctness / pass@k
Scoring outputs by whether they work — tests pass, SQL returns the right rows; pass@k is the chance at least one of k samples passes. See Evaluation methodology.

F–H#

Faithfulness (groundedness)
Whether every claim in an answer is supported by the retrieved context. See RAG evaluation.
Fine-tuning
Further training of a model’s weights on your examples. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.
GenAI adoption maturity
Stages from explore and experiment to formalise, scale and transform. See GenAI adoption strategy.
GOAP (goal-oriented action planning)
A planning algorithm from game AI that chains actions by preconditions and effects to reach a goal. See JVM frameworks.
Golden dataset
A versioned set of test cases with expected answers used for evaluation. See RAG evaluation.
GraphRAG
RAG over a knowledge graph of entities, relationships and community summaries. See GraphRAG.
Guardrails
Checks on inputs, actions and outputs that keep an AI system within policy. See Agent reliability.
Hallucination
Fluent but unsupported or false model output. See How LLMs work.
HNSW
A multi-layer graph index for fast approximate vector search. See Vector databases.
Human-in-the-loop (HITL)
Pausing an AI process for human approval, correction or input. See Workflow patterns.
Hybrid AI deployment
Some workloads on your own infrastructure, others on cloud models, under one control plane. See On-prem & hybrid.
Hybrid search
Combining vector and keyword search, usually fused with RRF. See Advanced retrieval.
HyDE
Searching with the embedding of an LLM-generated hypothetical answer. See Advanced retrieval.
Goodput
Requests per second that meet latency SLOs — the capacity you can actually offer. See Inference optimisation.

K–L#

KV cache
Stored attention keys and values that speed up generation. See Inference.
Lethal trifecta
Private data + untrusted content + external communication in one agent. See AI security.
LangGraph
A graph runtime for agents with durable checkpoints and interrupts. See Python & TypeScript frameworks.
LLM-as-a-judge
Using an LLM with a rubric to grade outputs. See RAG evaluation.
LLMOps
Practices for operating LLM applications. See LLMOps.
LoRA
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with small low-rank adapters. See Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.
Large reasoning model (LRM)
A model trained to reason step by step before answering, stronger at math, code and planning but slower and costlier. See Levels, SPAR & keystones.

M–N#

MCP (Model Context Protocol)
An open protocol for AI applications to use tools, resources and prompts from servers. See MCP.
Managed agent platform
A cloud service that runs agents with session isolation, memory, identity, tool gateways and observability. See Managed platforms.
Mixture of Experts (MoE)
A model architecture that routes each token to a few expert sub-networks. See How LLMs work.
Model routing
Sending each request to the cheapest capable model. See Model selection.
MRR / nDCG
Retrieval ranking metrics. See RAG evaluation.
Model risk management (MRM)
Banking discipline (SR 11-7, PRA SS1/23) for inventorying, validating and monitoring models, now applied to LLMs. See Hybrid AI in financial services.
Model-weight ownership
Who holds a model’s weights, deciding whether you can pin, move and keep it. See Hybrid AI in financial services.
NIST AI RMF
A risk-management framework with Govern, Map, Measure and Manage functions. See AI governance.
MFU / MBU
Model FLOPs utilisation and model bandwidth utilisation — how close a workload gets to the hardware’s peak compute and memory bandwidth. See Inference optimisation.
Model collapse
Loss of diversity and rare cases when models are trained repeatedly on model-generated data. See Dataset engineering.
Model merging
Combining fine-tuned models by averaging, interpolating or pruning their weights, without retraining. See Fine-tuning in depth.

O–R#

Orchestrator–workers
A central LLM dynamically delegating sub-tasks to workers. See Workflow patterns.
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
The ten most critical security risks for LLM apps. See AI security.
Prompt caching
Reusing computation for a repeated prompt prefix. See Inference.
Prompt injection
Input that makes a model follow attacker instructions. See AI security.
Quantization
Storing weights or vectors at lower precision to save memory. See Inference.
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)
Retrieving relevant passages and generating an answer grounded in them. See RAG fundamentals.
ReAct
An agent pattern interleaving reasoning, actions and observations. See What is an agent?
Reasoning model
A model trained to think step by step before answering. See How LLMs work.
RRF (reciprocal rank fusion)
Merging ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank). See Advanced retrieval.
PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning)
Training a small set of new or selected parameters (adapters, LoRA, soft prompts) while freezing the model. See Fine-tuning in depth.
Perplexity
The exponential of cross-entropy: how uncertain a model is when predicting text. See Evaluation methodology.
Prefill and decode
The two phases of generation: processing the prompt in parallel (compute-bound) and producing tokens one at a time (memory-bandwidth-bound). See Inference optimisation.
QLoRA
LoRA adapters trained on top of a base model quantised to 4 bits. See Fine-tuning in depth.
RLHF
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: train a reward model on human comparisons, then optimise the model against it. See Training, scaling & sampling.

S–Z#

Shadow AI
Staff using unapproved AI tools, often with company data. See GenAI adoption strategy.
Sovereign cloud
Cloud operated under local jurisdiction by a local entity and staff. See On-prem & hybrid.
Structured output
Model output constrained to a schema and parsed into types. See Prompt engineering.
Temperature
A sampling setting controlling randomness. See How LLMs work.
Token
The sub-word unit models read and write. See How LLMs work.
Token exchange (on-behalf-of)
An OAuth flow giving an agent a short-lived, scoped token to act for a user. See Agent identity.
Tool calling (function calling)
The model requesting your application to run a function. See Tool calling.
ToolContext (Spring AI)
Data passed to tools without exposing it to the model. See Spring AI tools.
Vector database
A store optimised for nearest-neighbour search over embeddings with filters. See Vector databases.
Zero data retention (ZDR)
Provider terms under which prompts and outputs are not stored after processing. See On-prem & hybrid.
Scaling law
The predictable fall in loss as parameters, data and compute grow; Chinchilla suggests about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training. See Training, scaling & sampling.
Semantic caching
Returning a stored answer for a query whose embedding is similar to a previous one. See AI engineering architecture.
SPAR
Sense, plan, act, reflect — the operating cycle of an agent. See Levels, SPAR & keystones.
Speculative decoding
A small draft model proposes tokens that the large model verifies in one pass, cutting latency without changing outputs. See Inference optimisation.
Synthetic data
Training or evaluation data generated by rules, simulation or models — useful for coverage, risky without verification. See Dataset engineering.
Test-time compute
Spending more inference compute per request — best-of-N, voting, reasoning tokens — to improve answers. See Training, scaling & sampling.
Tool resilience (control × impact)
Assessing agent tools by how much you control them and how critical they are; critical, low-control tools need fallbacks. See Levels, SPAR & keystones.
TTFT / TPOT
Time to first token and time per output token — the two latency numbers users feel. See Inference optimisation.
Usefulness threshold
The minimum quality, latency and cost at which an AI application is worth shipping. See AI engineering fundamentals.
